You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

pub fn engine_pattern(t: &str) -> String {

    let mut in_class = false;
    while i < chars.len() {
        let ch = chars[i];
        if ch == '\\' && i + 1 < chars.len() {
            out.push(ch);
            out.push(chars[i + 1]);
            i += 2;
            continue;
        }
        if ch == '[' && !in_class {

        } else if ch == ']' && in_class {

            continue;

I've reimplemented the CLI in Rust, and in my comparisons against the original binary it produces the same stdout and exit codes on everything except a few unusual corners (listed below). Everything is committed, and `./compile.sh` builds `./executable` from a fresh clone with an empty cargo home.

**How I checked it:** I wrote about 560 hand-made cases plus four random generators (thousands of random schemas, `$ref`/`$id` graphs, deliberately invalid schemas, and number edge cases), ran each through both binaries and compared output and exit code. The final runs of the hand-made suites and the number fuzzer had zero mismatches. The random schema generators still find roughly one mismatch per hundred or more cases, all in the corners below.

**What it covers:**
- **Command line:** the same flags, help text, version line and argument errors as the original (it uses the same argument-parsing library), the same order of checks, and the same messages on stdout. Panics and crashes give the same message on stderr and exit codes 101 and 134.
- **Validation:** all keywords for drafts 4, 6, 7, 2019-09 and 2020-12, with the original's error wording and ordering. That includes the original's bugs, which I copied on purpose:
  - Several `$anchor` references in one file all resolve to whichever anchor was looked up first.
  - `"items": false` makes `additionalItems` reject every instance.
  - A `properties`/`additionalProperties: false` combination always reports a single required property as missing if it isn't listed under `properties`.
- **Output formats:** text, flag, list and hierarchical, including the original's odd schema locations and annotations. It also reproduces the three paths for checking the schema itself, which treat `-d` differently.
- **Numbers:** arbitrary-precision handling that matches how the original compares and divides very large or very precise numbers.
- **Formats and regular expressions:** all formats with the original's per-draft availability. Patterns are translated the same way and match the original's rules for which patterns are accepted.

**Known differences:**
- **Remote `$ref` over http/https:** never fetched; it always reports the "error sending request" failure the original shows when there's no network.
- **Recursion:** some schemas mixing recursive `$ref`, `$dynamicRef` and anchors give a different result or report a different error first.
- **Regex:** variable-length lookbehind such as `(?<=a+)` and `\b{start}` are rejected in `pattern`, though the `regex` format check accepts them.
- **Missing external files:** when several referenced files are missing, the original reports a random one each run, so that case can't match reliably.

**Dependencies:** the code is my own. The general-purpose libraries (JSON, argument parsing, regex, IDNA) are vendored into `vendor/` (about 25 MB) so the offline build doesn't rely on the machine's package cache; none of them is the original project's code.

I never ran `compile.sh` inside `/workspace`: it overwrites `./executable`, which is still the original binary there. Build artifacts and `./executable` are in `.gitignore`.

I've reimplemented the jsonschema CLI (v0.41.0) from scratch in Rust. Across my differential tests it produces the same stdout and exit codes as the original. Everything is committed, and `./compile.sh` builds `./executable` from a fresh clone with an empty `CARGO_HOME`.

**How I checked it:** I compared it against the original binary on about 560 hand-written cases (CLI flags, all output modes, all drafts, refs, formats, invalid schemas, real-world-style schemas) and all pass. Five random fuzzers ran several thousand generated cases. The last full regression run matched on all of them except two, both described below. The only stderr output I compared was the panic and crash messages.

**What's covered:**
- **CLI:** built with the same `clap` library, so help text, usage lines and argument errors match. This includes the custom seconds parser, the version flag, `--errors-only`, the cacert check, and the original's panics (broken pipe, bad timeout values, paths that can't be resolved).
- **Order of steps:** text and structured output go through different sequences of schema checking and building, and those differ again with and without `-i`. I matched them.
- **Validation:** all keywords across drafts 4, 6, 7, 2019-09 and 2020-12, with the original's error messages, error order and evaluation order. Large and precise numbers are compared and checked for `multipleOf` the way the original does it, quirks included.
- **list / hierarchical output:** reproduces the original's internal structure, including its odd merged validators (e.g. `additionalProperties`/`properties`/`required`), annotations versus dropped annotations, and its location strings.
- **References:** `$ref`, `$dynamicRef`, `$recursiveRef`, `$id` and anchors, local files fetched with `file://`, and recursion cut-offs at the same depth.
- **Original's bugs reproduced deliberately:**
  - Anchor targets in one resource get mixed up, because the original caches them under the same location.
  - Schemas that make the original overflow its stack (cycles involving `unevaluated*`) abort the same way.
  - `"items": false` alongside `additionalItems` rejects every instance.
- **Formats and regexes:**
  - All formats are implemented; `idn-hostname` uses the `idna` crate plus context rules.
  - Content encodings: base64, base64url, base32, base16.
  - ECMA regexes are translated to the same patterns the original shows in its error messages, with its stricter syntax rules.

**Known gaps:**
- **No network:** `http(s)` refs are never fetched. They give the same "error sending request for url (…)" message the original shows when it can't connect, so anything that relies on a real download will differ.
- **Two `pattern` features:** variable-length lookbehind and `\b{start}` are rejected as invalid, while the original accepts them.
- **Some unusual reference setups:** schemas mixing `$dynamicRef` or several `#anchor` refs with cycles, or relative pointers across `$id` resources, can still report a different first error or different nested output. These are the two remaining fuzzer mismatches.
- **Retrieval order:** when several referenced files are missing, the original reports one picked at random on each run, so no single expected output exists.

All third-party crates are vendored in `vendor/` (about 25 MB) so the build needs no network. They are generic libraries (`serde_json`, `clap`, `regex`, `fancy-regex`, `idna`), not jsonschema code. Build output and `./executable` are in `.gitignore`. Running `./compile.sh` in `/workspace` will replace the original binary there, so I didn't run it in place.
